name: Determining Whether One is a Teenager (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that receives a string that has the user name and age separated by a colon, and prints whether the user is a teenager. Make sure that the program handles all possible exceptions.
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def check_age(s):
    #Step 1.1: Split the given string into the name and age 
    lst = s.split(":")
    #Step 1.2: Enclose the code that might throw an exception within the try block
    try:
        name = lst[0]
        age = int(lst[1])
        if age >= 13 and age <= 19 :            
            print(name + " is a teenager.")
        else:            
            print(name + " is not a teenager.")     
    #Step 1.3: Handle all possible exceptions that may be thrown in the try block 
    except IndexError :
        print("Error! Separate the name and age by a colon.")
    except ValueError :
        print("Error! Age must be an integer.")
#Step 2: Call the function
check_age(input("Enter the name and age, separated by a colon:"))

commentList: Purpose: This line asks the user to type the name and age, then passes what the user typed to the check_age function so the program can decide and print whether that person is a teenager. You need this call to actually run the function using real input.

Syntax and evaluation: input("Enter the name and age, separated by a colon:") displays the prompt and returns a string; that returned string is then given as the single argument to check_age(...). The input() call runs first, then check_age is called with its result.

Common errors and misconceptions: if the user types a string without a colon, the function will raise an IndexError when it tries to access the age part—your function already handles that. If the user types a non-integer age, ValueError will be raised and is handled. However, input() itself can raise EOFError (Ctrl+D) or KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C), which are not handled here, so the program could stop unexpectedly if the user cancels input.

Best practices: to make this more robust, you could first store the input in a variable so you can inspect or reuse it (e.g., user_input = input(...)), wrap the input() call in a try/except to catch EOFError/KeyboardInterrupt, and trim extra spaces with user_input.strip() before calling check_age. Inside check_age you can also use s.split(':', 1) to allow colons in the name and avoid splitting more than once.

Practical note on behavior: remember that int() will accept surrounding spaces (e.g., ' 15 ') so you usually don't need to strip the age for conversion, but you should still strip the name if you want clean output. Also remember that the prompt string only appears once — check_age will not be called until the user presses Enter.

distractors.description: Step-by-step why you might pick this: you may remember that Python raises different error types when things go wrong and think TypeError sounds like a general 'wrong type' error that fits converting a string to int. You might also conflate operations on wrong types with failed conversions and assume TypeError will catch the problem. How this affects the program: int('abc') raises a ValueError, not a TypeError. If you use this line, the ValueError from the failed int conversion will not be caught here and the program will crash with an uncaught ValueError. That means the user sees a traceback instead of a friendly error message. Why this is invalid: this line listens for the wrong exception class. Compared to the intended specific handler for conversion failures, it is too narrow in the wrong way — it looks for TypeError instead of the actual exception class thrown by int(), so it fails to handle the real error you expect to catch.

Step-by-step why you might pick this: you may want a simple catch-all so any error is handled and think using a bare except is an easy shortcut. You might believe it guarantees the program always prints a friendly message for any bad input. How this affects the program: a bare except will catch every exception, including IndexError, ValueError, KeyboardInterrupt, and even system-exiting exceptions. That means an IndexError will be reported with the same message intended for age conversion errors, which is misleading. It will also hide other bugs and make debugging harder. In short, the program will not distinguish different problems and may mask serious issues. Why this is invalid: this line is too broad — it swallows all exceptions instead of handling the specific error you expect, so you lose useful information and give the user the wrong feedback for different failure cases.

You might think re-raising an exception makes the problem clearer to whoever is debugging the program. Step-by-step: 1) When the IndexError is caught, this line deliberately raises another IndexError instead of handling it. 2) Because nothing else in the program catches this new exception, the program will terminate and print a traceback. 3) The user experience is worse: instead of a friendly, handled message, the user sees a crash and a stack trace. Why this is invalid: an exception handler should recover or present a clear, user-facing message, not re-raise an error that will stop the program. Using this line prevents graceful handling and confuses end users.
